newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs more reform to match E.Asia - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: India needs more reform to match E.Asia - World Bank.

text.p: India has spurred economic growth with a "quiet economic revolution" launched in 1991, but more tough steps are needed for it to match its East Asian neighbours' success, the World Bank said on Wednesday.
"The Indian economy is on the move," World Bank vice president D. Joseph Wood said in a statement accompanying an annual report on the Indian economy by the Washington-based bank.

The 220-page report urges official and private donors, due to meet in Tokyo on September 18-20, to support India's liberalisation programme with increased long-term development assistance, including loans at concessional rates.
"The stabilisation and reform measures introduced over the past five years have considerably improved India's growth prospects," the report said.
But the bank said "strong additional measures are required for India to match the high East Asian growth rates of seven percent or more", and offered a long list of recommendations.

The foremost priority, it said, was for India to get budgetary red ink under control to bring down high interest rates "which pose a threat to the sustainability of the recovery and the soundness of the banking system".

The bank lauded Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's new centre-left government for vowing to rein in the fiscal deficit to 5.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1996/97 financial year which began on April 1, from 5.9 percent in 1995/96.

But it said previous governments had failed to meet deficit targets, and cautioned that measures spelled out in the budget blueprint which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram presented to parliament in July could miss the mark.
"Some of the assumptions underlying both the revenue and the expenditure forecasts may be over-optimistic," it said. Parliament is expected to approve the budget by mid-September.
Instead, New Delhi should aim to slash the deficit to 3.5 percent of GDP to avoid a slowdown in economic growth and a rise in inflation, it said.
The bank recommended that the government cut subsidies, allow the number of state workers to shrink, broaden the tax base and raise the price of power for farmers and households.
It urged India to overhaul farm programmes, lower tariffs, privatise public banks, deregulate insurance and cut both corporate tax rates and exemptions.
"India is facing an imminent crisis in infrastructure," it said, urging the government to press ahead with opening up power, roads, ports and other capital-intensive sectors to private investment.
The bank said the five-year-old reform programme may have created the preconditions for India's economy to grow at a stable six to seven percent a year.
But to meet its huge infrastructure needs, India will need long-term development assistance from outside donors, both official and private, the bank said.
The World Bank said India will need $8 billion in financing in 1996 from the Aid Coordinating Group of Donors meeting in Tokyo next month, up from $6.5 billion last year.
It will need an average of $13 billion in each of the following four years, the bank said.
